definitions.meaning: The distribution of a statistic, such as the sample mean, over many repeated samples of the same size: the sample means cluster around the true mean, with standard deviation sigma / root n.
A procedure that states a null hypothesis H0 and an alternative H1, then rejects H0 when the observed data would be sufficiently surprising if H0 were true.
The probability, computed assuming H0 is true, of getting data at least as extreme as the data observed: if H0 were true, a p-value of 0.03 means 3% of experiments would give data this extreme.
The threshold alpha, often 0.05, fixed before the test: reject H0 when the p-value is smaller than alpha. Alpha also caps the probability of a Type I error.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis - a false alarm. Its probability is alpha, the significance level chosen in advance.
Accepting a false null hypothesis - a missed signal. Its probability is beta, and the power of the test, 1 - beta, is the chance of avoiding it.

mechanismSteps: The sampling distribution of the mean shrinks as n grows: sample means cluster around the true mean, and as n grows from 2 to 25 the distribution of those means gets taller and narrower, because the spread shrinks by root n.
Hypothesis testing: the p-value decides against α: state H0 and H1, shade the tail beyond the observed statistic to read the p-value, and reject H0 exactly when that p-value falls below alpha = 0.05.
The p-value trap: it is not P(H₀ is true): repeat the test 100 times while H0 is true and about 3 repeats land in the extreme tail - that count of repeats is all the p-value of 0.03 says.

Type I and Type II errors: the two ways to be wrong: lay reality across the top and the decision down the side - rejecting a true null is the Type I false alarm capped by alpha, and accepting a false null is the Type II missed signal fought with power.
objectives: Describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean and compute its standard deviation as sigma / root n
Carry out a hypothesis test by comparing the p-value with the significance level alpha
State what a p-value does and does not measure, avoiding the trap reading

trap.explanation: The p-value is read as a probability about the hypothesis itself. The p-value is about the data given the null: if H0 were true, 3% of experiments would give data this extreme. The p-value is computed in the world where H0 is true, so it measures the data's surprise in that world - repeating the test 100 times under H0, about 3 repeats give data this extreme. It never assigns a probability to H0 itself.
trap.misconception: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.

workedExample: Work with a population of mean 60 and standard deviation 10. For samples of size n = 25, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is centred on 60 with standard deviation 10 / root 25 = 10 / 5 = 2, so sample means typically land within a few units of 60. Now test H0: the mean is 60 against H1: the mean exceeds 60, at the 5% level. The test returns p = 0.03. Compare p with alpha: 0.03 is smaller than 0.05, so reject H0 - the data would be surprising if the null were true. Note carefully what was not shown: the p-value 0.03 is not the probability that H0 is true.
